glossary.thirteenF: A quarterly disclosure the US SEC requires from large managers (>$100M AUM). Filed up to 45 days after quarter-end, it shows only long positions in US-listed stocks.
glossary.putCall: Put/Call are options. Put = right to sell at a set price; Call = right to buy. Most guru portfolios are plain long stock; options are a small part.
glossary.yoy: Year-over-year, change vs. the same month last year, removing seasonality.
glossary.mom: Month-over-month, change vs. the previous month (short-term momentum).
glossary.drip: Dividend Reinvestment Plan: automatically using dividends to buy more shares, compounding your returns.
glossary.per: How many years to earn back the price if you bought the whole company. A shop earning $10k/yr bought for $100k → 10 years → PER 10. Low = cheap (or the market doubts its future); high = expensive (or high hopes priced in). Only meaningful vs. peers in the same sector.
glossary.pbr: Price vs. what shareholders would get if the company shut down and sold everything (net assets). Buying a shop with $100k of assets for $100k = PBR 1. Below 1 = cheaper than its asset value; above 1 = priced above assets.
glossary.forwardPer: PER uses last year's profit; forward PER uses this/next year's expected profit. If profits are expected to grow, forward PER comes out lower. It's a PER that reflects future expectations.
glossary.psr: A price multiple based on revenue, not profit. Used for fast-growing companies not yet profitable. Lower = cheaper relative to sales.
glossary.peg: PER divided by profit growth rate. Judges whether a stock is expensive after accounting for growth, around 1 is often seen as fair, lower as cheap for the growth. Helps make sense of a high PER on a fast grower.
glossary.eps: Earnings per share, the net profit one share earned in a year (total profit ÷ shares). Bigger, and rising each year, is better. It's the basis of the PER calculation.
glossary.bps: Book value per share, the net assets (assets − debt) behind one share; the theoretical amount a share would get on liquidation. Price ÷ BPS = PBR.
glossary.dividendYield: What % you get back in dividends per year at today's price, think of it like a bank interest rate. E.g. price $100, annual dividend $3 → 3%. Higher isn't always better; check that the company earns enough to sustain it.
glossary.marketCap: The whole company's price tag = share price × total shares. The amount it would take to buy the entire company. Bigger = large cap, smaller = small cap.
glossary.price: The price of one share currently trading in the market.
glossary.revenue: Total money brought in from selling goods/services, the 'gross sales' before costs. What matters is whether it keeps growing.
glossary.operatingIncome: Profit left after subtracting the costs of doing business (materials, wages, etc.) from revenue. Shows how much the core business actually made.
glossary.netIncome: The profit finally left after taxes and interest, the real 'take-home'. It's the basis for EPS and PER.
glossary.totalAssets: The sum of everything the company owns (cash, plants, inventory, etc.). Made up of its own money (equity) plus borrowed money (liabilities).
glossary.totalLiabilities: The total debt the company must repay. Too large relative to assets can be a warning sign.
glossary.equity: Assets minus liabilities, the portion purely owned by shareholders. It's the basis for BPS.
glossary.cfOperating: Cash that actually came in and went out through the core business. Book profit means little if cash doesn't follow, so steady positive is what matters.
glossary.cfInvesting: Cash spent on or recovered from equipment, stakes, etc. Investing for growth usually makes this negative (cash goes out).
glossary.cfFinancing: Cash moved by borrowing/repaying and by dividends/buybacks. Repaying debt and paying dividends make it negative.
glossary.freeCashFlow: The cash truly free to use after subtracting essential investment from operating cash. It's the source of dividends, buybacks and debt repayment, steadily positive means a sturdy company.
glossary.movingAverage: A line joining the average of the last N days' closing prices. It smooths out choppy prices to show the average trend. The 5-day line = short-term, the 120-day = long-term; shorter lines react faster to recent prices.
glossary.fromHigh: How far below the period's highest price the current price sits (drawdown). e.g. −20% means it has fallen 20% from the peak, a sense of how much it has pulled back.
glossary.fromLow: How far above the period's lowest price the current price sits (rebound). e.g. +30% means it has risen 30% off the bottom.

tech.chartSub: Daily OHLC with simple moving averages (SMA) 5, 20, 60, 120D
tech.maHint: Moving Average (MA) = a line connecting the average closing price of the last N days. MA20 ≈ the average price over the last 20 days, smoothing the trend. Bigger numbers (60, 120) show longer trends; smaller (5, 20) show recent moves. Tap a line to toggle it.
tech.beginnerHint: Showing key indicators only — tap 'Advanced' to see moving averages, RSI and more.
tech.nearSrHint: Zones where price has repeatedly stalled or bounced. Not an exact line but a range, and they can break at any time. Not a buy/sell signal.
tech.pos52Hint: Where the current price sits between the 1-year low and high. Near the high doesn't mean a ceiling, nor near the low a floor.
tech.atrHint: Roughly how much this stock moves in a typical day (based on ATR) — a feel for what counts as normal wiggle.
tech.turnoverHint: Money traded today, estimated as close × volume. May differ slightly from the exchange's official turnover.
tech.squeezeHint: Bollinger bandwidth is at its narrowest recently. A big move can follow quiet periods, but this doesn't tell you the direction.
tech.signalsSub: State read from past prices, for reference
tech.alignBullishNote: Short-term MAs sit above longer ones in order, typically read as an uptrend.
tech.alignBearishNote: Short-term MAs sit below longer ones, typically read as a downtrend.
tech.alignMixedNote: Moving averages are intertwined; the trend is weak here.
tech.alignHint: When the MAs line up short→long from the top (5>20>60>120) it's a bullish alignment, an uptrend has settled in. The reverse (long line on top) is a bearish alignment, a downtrend.
tech.crossGoldenNote: The 5-day line crossed above the 20-day, read as a short-term upturn signal.
tech.crossDeadNote: The 5-day line crossed below the 20-day, read as a short-term downturn signal.
tech.crossHint: Golden cross = the short line (5-day) breaks up through the long line (20-day), momentum strengthening, an upturn hope. Dead cross = it breaks down through, momentum fading, a downturn worry. It's a lagging reference, so it can trail the actual move.
tech.posNote: How far the price has stretched from its moving average, in %.
tech.posHint: Disparity = price ÷ MA × 100. 100 = right on the average; well above (≥110) = short-term overheated (watch for a pullback); well below (≤90) = oversold (room to rebound). Rule of thumb on the 20-day line.
tech.rsiHint: RSI(14) maps the ratio of recent gains to losses over 14 days onto a 0-100 scale. Above 70 is short-term overbought, below 30 is oversold. Extremes can hint at a reversal.
tech.rsiNote: 50 is the neutral line. Higher values mean the recent rise was steeper.
tech.tfHint: The slope of the long (120-day), mid (60-day) and short (20-day) moving averages shows each horizon's direction. Check whether the long-term trend is intact before judging the short-term move. (All based on the same daily candles.)
tech.tfNote: A short-term dip is more reliable when the long-term direction points up.
tech.volHint: Moves backed by volume reflect real demand. This compares volume on up-days vs down-days over the last 10 sessions to see where the weight is. Heavy volume with a long upper wick near highs warns of a trend ending.
tech.vixHint: VIX is the fear gauge for the whole US market (not this stock). Above 40 is extreme fear, historically a good buying opportunity; below 20 is complacency. Use it only as backdrop for market mood.
tech.disclaimer: These signals are a state reading based on past prices and moving averages (reference only) and are not a recommendation to buy or sell. Moving averages are lagging indicators; past trends do not guarantee future returns.

macro.ratePrinciple: Combines the Fed's dual mandate (inflation + employment) with market expectations (2Y Treasury, yield curve). Inflation above the 2% target and rising leans hike; a cooling labor market leans cut. This is a rule-based reading of public indicators, not a forecast of any decision and not investment advice.
macro.rateUnavailable: Could not load the rate direction.
macro.assetHoldNote: Neutral zone, no clear direction. On the cut side growth stocks, gold and bonds tend to benefit; on the hike side the dollar and financials.
macro.assetCaveat: Historical tendencies with many exceptions (expectations get priced in, supply shocks, etc.). Not investment advice.
